title: A New Kind Of Creative Poverty | NOEMA
gist: The essay argues that LLM alignment/training produces the same flattened, 'safe' outputs as China's censored 'Simplified Chinese Internet,' and uses Baudelaire's prosecuted, transgressive 'Les Fleurs du mal' to argue that Silicon Valley's new obsession with 'taste' will itself calcify into another form of algorithmic sameness.

themes.theme: AI Slop And The Collapse Of Reader Trust

insights.claim: Writers report a strong visceral aversion to identifiable AI writing tells such as 'tapestry,' 'crystallize,' 'delve,' and the construction 'it's not X, it's Y,' which read as a low-effort, overfitted register.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Signals a maturing, quantifiable backlash market against AI-generated text that detection-tool and 'human-verified' content products are already monetizing.
insights.quote: “tapestry,” “crystallize,” “delve,” or “it’s not X, it’s Y” — that low-effort, overfitted register.
insights.locator: Almost every writer I know has some visceral repulsion

insights.claim: British writer Sam Kriss expressed extreme hostility toward AI-generated writing in an essay titled 'If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you,' describing constant paranoid vigilance about whether any given piece of writing is secretly machine-generated.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Illustrates how emotionally charged (not just aesthetic) the anti-AI-writing backlash has become among professional writers.
insights.quote: I hate it. I find it viscerally disgusting; a cold shudder like someone’s poured jelly down the back of my neck.
insights.locator: Sam Kriss, essay titled 'If you let AI do your writing'

insights.claim: Substack and LessWrong were both originally built on the assumption that readers could trust the writing in front of them to be authentic and human, an assumption the essay says no longer holds today.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A foundational trust assumption underlying user-generated content platforms has broken, forcing product-level responses rather than just cultural griping.
insights.quote: Today, that assumption no longer holds.
insights.locator: Chris Best, Substack's chief executive, and Oliver Habryka

insights.claim: LessWrong now requires writers to disclose AI use, and Substack has launched Pangram-style AI-detection features to curb 'Claudefishing' so readers don't unknowingly give their attention to text with no human thought behind it.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that AI-detection is becoming built-in platform infrastructure, not just a fringe reader habit — a potential product category and moat for publishing platforms.
insights.quote: so readers don’t “unwittingly invest their attention in something with no human thought on the other end.”
insights.locator: LessWrong now requires its writers to disclose

insights.claim: LinkedIn is cited as a platform already so saturated with AI-generated slop that users openly mock it, exemplifying a broader tech-industry backlash against soulless AI content.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Shows early, visible market disillusionment on a major professional platform that could pressure it toward authenticity features or reputational damage.
insights.quote: LinkedIn, for instance, has become a dumpster of AI slop people laugh at
insights.locator: The tech industry's actions and inaction

insights.claim: People generating fiction with LLMs have noticed an outsized share of resulting stories are about lighthouses, clockmakers, and librarians, disproportionately featuring a protagonist named 'Elias Thorne,' a name now recurring across self-published Amazon books, fake news sites, and YouTube videos.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable symptom of LLM output homogenization that is already visibly polluting downstream content ecosystems (self-publishing, low-quality media).
insights.quote: a disproportionate number of stories about lighthouses, clockmakers and librarians — and these stories would always feature a protagonist named “Elias Thorne.”
insights.locator: many people using LLMs to write stories

insights.claim: This repetition is described as a concrete instance of model collapse, defined as a failure state where a model produces repetitive, low-diversity output.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Names a specific failure mode investors and builders in generative AI should track as a quality/diversity risk in model outputs.
insights.quote: It’s a typical phenomenon of model collapse — a failure state where a model produces repetitive, low-diversity outputs.
insights.locator: It's a typical phenomenon of model collapse

insights.claim: One offered explanation (flagged as an unverified guess) is that alignment causes LLMs to prefer the safest outputs during post-training, avoiding anything low-reward such as inappropriate content or copyright infringement, which pushes the model to maximize reward rather than originality.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Suggests the very safety/reward mechanisms companies build into models may be a direct structural cause of creative homogenization, a tension for any AI-content business model.
insights.quote: An LLM will avoid every possible minefield and choose outputs that maximize the reward within its system parameters
insights.locator: One unverified guess is that alignment

insights.claim: The author compares AI homogenization to Chinese Gaokao exam essays, where an 18-year-old student under exam pressure defaults to the same safe canonical references — Lu Xun, Helen Keller, Madame Curie, Qian Xuesen and Du Fu — because that cookie-cutter, morality-driven package reliably earns a good score.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Draws a direct structural parallel between exam-driven human conformity and reward-driven AI conformity, implying both are products of scoring/optimization regimes rather than genuine creative constraint.
insights.quote: the result is a cookie-cutter lineup of Lu Xun, Helen Keller, Madame Curie, Qian Xuesen and Du Fu — morality-driven, legible packages that reliably earn a good Gaokao score.
insights.locator: It's almost like asking an 18-year-old Chinese student

insights.claim: Jerry Zhou, a friend who worked on LLM training at Microsoft AI, frames a model as functionally a single person that millions of people worldwide are simultaneously questioning; because the questions are similar, the answers converge, and the model won't surprise or shock anyone unless someone intervenes at the level of model weights or the training objective.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A practitioner-sourced mental model for why scale itself (millions of similar queries to one 'person') mechanically produces convergence — useful shorthand for evaluating any large deployed model's output diversity.
insights.quote: unless you intervene at the level of the LLM weights or training objective, you should never expect this person to surprise you, and especially not shock you.
insights.locator: My friend Jerry Zhou

themes.theme: The Simplified Chinese Internet As LLM Training Analogy

insights.claim: The essay's central analogy is that the 'Simplified Chinese Internet' (简中互联网) — a version of Chinese online language flattened by years of shrinking discussion space, algorithm-favored brevity, and censorship — is the product of the same kind of long-running reward-and-punishment environment that resembles today's LLM training.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Frames AI alignment as structurally continuous with authoritarian information control, a lens investors in AI-safety and content-moderation tooling should weigh when assessing long-run creative/output quality.
insights.quote: the language used on it can be understood as the product of a long reward-and-punishment environment that resembles today’s LLM training.
insights.locator: Escaping The Simplified Chinese Internet

insights.claim: The author argues censorship does not itself generate creativity: the 2022 'White Paper' protests, where demonstrators held blank paper against Zero-COVID because the state and its algorithms cannot censor emptiness, are the exception rather than proof that authoritarian control fosters ingenuity, since most people deemed 'unsafe' simply left the Simplified Chinese Internet or went idle.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a romanticized 'constraint breeds creativity' narrative that could otherwise be misapplied to argue AI guardrails spur rather than suppress originality.
insights.quote: such cleverness is not a credit to censorship itself, or evidence that authoritarian control doesn’t suffocate creativity and self-expression. That conclusion would be utterly wrong.
insights.locator: The 2022 'White Paper' protests

themes.theme: Baudelaire: Transgression As The Origin Of Greatness

insights.claim: Charles Baudelaire's 'Les Fleurs du mal' was prosecuted by French authorities the moment it appeared in the summer of 1857 on charges of blasphemy and outrage to public decency; he was convicted of indecency and six poems were ordered removed from the book, with the conviction formally overturned only on May 31, 1949.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A near-century gap between prosecution and vindication is used as a concrete historical benchmark for how long society can take to recognize genius that violated its 'safety' norms.
insights.quote: he was convicted for indecency, and six of his poems were ordered removed from the book.
insights.locator: Baudelaire was prosecuted the instant

insights.claim: Baudelaire's method was to pour morally transgressive content into the strictest inherited forms of French verse — the alexandrine, the quatrain, the sonnet — so that inside orderly, expected meter the reader does not find the themes the form trains them to expect; the resulting shock is the point of the work.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Offers a reusable model for how genuine artistic disruption works — subverting content inside a trusted, legible structure — as the opposite of AI's tendency to keep both form and content safely predictable.
insights.quote: Inside those orderly meters the reader does not find the themes the form trains you to expect. Shock is the point.
insights.locator: All that moral trespass, he had poured

insights.claim: Critic Walter Benjamin cast Baudelaire as the forerunner of the modern poet because he captured, through the 'shocking, raw immediacy of his sense impressions,' an emergent urban commodity-capitalist reality that 19th-century Paris had no existing language to describe.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Ties artistic transgression directly to the ability to name and process genuinely new economic/social conditions before mainstream language catches up.
insights.quote: the “shocking, raw immediacy of his sense impressions” of that reality
insights.locator: The great 20th-century critic Walter Benjamin

insights.claim: Researcher Zhengdong Wang's observation about evaluating AI capability — 'we don't even know what we really want until we see it, at which point it may change' — is applied by the author to society's historical blindness to genius, since the world did not know it wanted a Baudelaire until it eventually understood him.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A cross-domain insight: benchmarking desire (for AI outputs or for art) is inherently retrospective, which undercuts confidence in current AI evaluation frameworks as predictors of true value.
insights.quote: We don’t even know what we really want until we see it, at which point it may change.
insights.locator: The blind spot the researcher Zhengdong Wang names

insights.claim: The author connects poet Bei Dao, who secretly preserved Baudelaire as a spiritual icon during China's Cultural Revolution, to his later founding of the Misty Poetry movement in more open 1980s China — a movement explicitly set against the socialist-realist, 'positive emotion' benchmarks the Cultural Revolution had prized.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Shows a real historical pathway from suppressed underground influence to a full counter-movement once political constraints loosened, a template for how creative reaction can lag but eventually surface.
insights.quote: was filled with the unknowable and the unforeseen.
insights.locator: Bei Dao, the poet who kept Baudelaire

themes.theme: Silicon Valley's 'Taste' Discourse As The Next Cliché

insights.claim: Silicon Valley has recently elevated 'taste' as the supposed antidote to AI-generated sameness, with an Atlantic article claiming taste is a competitive advantage for leaders and AI entrepreneurs describing taste as 'the new moat.'
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Identifies 'taste' as an emerging competitive-positioning narrative in AI-adjacent business discourse, comparable to prior buzzwords used to justify differentiation claims.
insights.quote: Taste is the new moat, these AI entrepreneurs say.
insights.locator: For leaders, 'taste is a competitive advantage'

insights.claim: The author predicts Silicon Valley's celebration of 'good taste' will itself calcify into a new mediocrity and predictability, comparing its likely trajectory to how 'disruption' became a hollow cliché in the 2010s, and notes the same 'good taste' talk has already spread to China's AI industry.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Warns that a currently fashionable differentiation narrative in AI branding/strategy circles is likely to lose its meaning and become just another marketing cliché rather than a durable moat.
insights.quote: Some of this “good taste” will soon become the new mid-curve of mediocrity, the new predictability, the new “it’s not X, it’s Y.”
insights.locator: My internal seismograph reads otherwise.

insights.claim: Baudelaire himself explicitly prized bad taste, writing in his private journals that what is exhilarating in bad taste is the aristocratic pleasure of giving offense — directly at odds with treating refined 'good taste' as the answer to flattened AI content.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Offers a historical counter-example undermining the premise that curated 'good taste' is the antidote to algorithmic sameness — the opposite instinct produced more lasting art.
insights.quote: “What is exhilarating in bad taste,” he wrote in his private journals, “is the aristocratic pleasure of giving offense.”
insights.locator: Baudelaire would have no use for it.

insights.claim: Claude's published 'Constitution,' an approximately 80-page document instructing the model how to behave, tells it to be 'genuinely good, wise, and virtuous' and to help people 'in the way a good person would,' a safety-alignment target the author argues is fundamentally incompatible with the kind of transgressive genius Baudelaire represents.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Names the specific alignment document and language behind a leading model's behavior, framing it as a direct, traceable source of the 'flattened' output the essay critiques.
insights.quote: instructs it to be “genuinely good, wise, and virtuous”: to be tactful, helpful, graceful, honest and, above all, to “help people in the way a good person would.”
insights.locator: Claude's own 'Constitution,'

insights.claim: Historian Simon Schama's line that 'great art has dreadful manners' — describing art as a 'thug' that will grab you in a headlock and rearrange your sense of reality — is invoked as a standard that alignment-trained, safety-optimized AI output structurally cannot meet.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Provides a memorable, quotable benchmark for what 'good' art actually does, against which safety-optimized AI content is implicitly measured and found lacking.
insights.quote: great art has dreadful manners.
insights.locator: I keep returning to a line from Simon Schama's

themes.theme: The Author's Own Entanglement With AI

insights.claim: As a non-native English speaker, the author relies heavily on Claude as a grammar checker to smooth her sentences and remove 'ESL flavor,' comparing the effect to installing a pair of mechanical wings that extend her reach to new audiences while making her writing feel less entirely her own.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Complicates a simple anti-AI-writing stance by showing AI-as-tool can be a genuine access enabler for non-native writers even while introducing a felt loss of authenticity.
insights.quote: AI makes those wings less heavy, but more not-entirely-me.
insights.locator: Because English is my second language

insights.claim: Noema discloses that this article's initial draft used Claude to improve grammar and syntax and that the piece then received numerous human edits plus a human fact-check and identity verification, illustrating one publication's concrete protocol for authorized AI use.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A working, disclosed example of a publisher's AI-use policy that other media outlets could benchmark against as disclosure norms solidify industry-wide.
insights.quote: The initial submitted draft of this piece used Claude to improve grammar and syntax. This piece has since received numerous human edits.
insights.locator: Editor's Note: Noema is transparent
